title: Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah: Justice and Hope
bigQuestion: What did the prophets say to the powerful, and why do readers still reach for their words?

story.title: One Verse, Two Crowds
story.kicker: A line first spoken at a northern shrine around 760 BCE was read aloud again in Washington, D.C., in 1963.
paragraphs: Picture the shrine at Bethel, in the northern kingdom of Israel, in about 760 BCE. The book of Amos sets its scene here. Worshippers bring animals and grain. Music plays. Trade is good, and the king, Jeroboam II, has made the country wealthy. Then a stranger from the south begins to speak. He is a herdsman from Tekoa, in Judah. He says that the feasts and songs mean nothing while the poor are sold for the price of a pair of sandals.

The book records the reaction. Amaziah, the priest at Bethel, tells Amos to go home to Judah and earn his bread there. Amos answers that he never trained as a prophet; he was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore figs, and God took him from the flock. Then he repeats his message. Near the middle of the book is the line readers remember most: let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream (Amos 5:24).

Now move ahead about 2,700 years. On August 28, 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. stands on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial before some 250,000 people. In the speech known as "I Have a Dream," he says the movement will not be satisfied until, in the prophet's words, justice rolls down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream. He does not name Amos. He does not need to. Many in the crowd knew the verse from church.

King was a Baptist minister who had studied the prophets in seminary. He quoted Amos again that same year in his "Letter from Birmingham Jail," calling Amos an extremist for justice. In 1966 he brought his campaign to Chicago, marching for open housing on the city's West and Southwest sides. The words of a herdsman from Tekoa had traveled a long way.

This chapter reads the prophets close up. They are not fortune tellers. In the Hebrew Bible a prophet is a messenger who delivers a word to a people and its leaders, often a hard word about how the poor are treated. Amos, Hosea, Micah, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel each speak into a real crisis. They also use forms of speech you can learn to spot. And their words have been read, and read differently, by Jews and Christians ever since.
story.think: Why might a speaker in 1963 choose a line from 760 BCE instead of writing a new one? What does an old text add to a new argument?

lessons.title: What a Prophet Is
lessons.mainIdea: In the Hebrew Bible a prophet is a messenger who delivers God's word to a people and its rulers, often as a challenge.
reading: The English word *prophet* comes from a Greek word meaning "one who speaks for" another. The Hebrew word is *navi*. In the Hebrew Bible a prophet is not mainly a predictor of the future. A prophet is a messenger who says, "Thus says the LORD," and then delivers a message to a king, a priest or a whole nation. The message often points at the present: how the poor are treated, whom the people trust, what the leaders are doing.

The books of the prophets sit in the second part of the Jewish Bible, the *Nevi'im*. Jewish tradition counts the "Former Prophets" (Joshua through Kings) and the "Latter Prophets" (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve). Christian Bibles group the same books differently, placing the prophets at the end of the Old Testament. The three long books are often called the Major Prophets and the twelve short ones the Minor Prophets. "Minor" means shorter, not less important.

Most of the writing prophets spoke between about 760 BCE and 500 BCE. That is the age when the Assyrian and then the Babylonian empires rose and crushed the small kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Many scholars read the prophets as voices from inside those crises. The books are mostly poetry, gathered and edited over time, and they name their speakers, their kings and sometimes their years. That lets readers place them on a map and a timeline.

words.d: in the Hebrew Bible, a messenger who delivers God's word to a people and its leaders; Hebrew navi
the Prophets, the second of the three parts of the Jewish Bible (Tanakh)
a message a prophet delivers as God's word, often beginning with "Thus says the LORD"
the twelve short prophetic books, called the Twelve in Jewish tradition; minor means shorter

look.title: When the Prophets Spoke
look.cite: Dates as commonly given in introductions to the Hebrew Bible; all are approximate (c.)
look.prompt: Which prophets spoke while Assyria was the great power (before c. 612 BCE), and which spoke in the Babylonian age?

check.q: In the Hebrew Bible, what is a prophet mainly?
choices: A messenger who delivers God's word to a people and its leaders
A priest who offers sacrifices at the temple
A king who rules by divine right
check.why: A navi is a messenger; the books focus on the message to the present, not mainly on predicting the future.

check.q: What does "Minor" mean in the phrase "Minor Prophets"?
check.why: The twelve books are called minor because they are short; Jewish tradition calls them simply the Twelve.

check.q: Which empire rose during the time of Amos and Isaiah of Jerusalem?
check.why: The eighth-century prophets spoke as Assyria expanded; Babylon came later, in the age of Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

lessons.title: Amos and the Poor
lessons.mainIdea: Amos says worship is worthless while the poor are cheated, and calls for justice to flow like a river.
reading: The book of Amos opens by dating itself to the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, about 760 BCE. Israel was prosperous. Amos, a herdsman from the southern town of Tekoa, traveled north to Bethel and spoke against that prosperity. His charge is specific. The rich, he says, sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6). They lie on ivory beds, drink wine by the bowlful, and take bribes in the courts.

Amos does not say that worship is wrong. He says that worship without *justice* is an insult. In chapter 5 the text has God say that he hates the people's feasts and will not accept their offerings or listen to their songs. Then comes the demand: let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like a strong, steady stream. Justice here means fair courts and fair dealing, especially for people with no power to fight back.

The book also uses a form scholars call the oracle against the nations. Chapters 1 and 2 pronounce judgment on Israel's neighbors one by one: Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab. A listener at Bethel might have cheered. Then Amos turns the same words on Judah and, last and longest, on Israel itself. The rhetoric traps the audience. Jewish and Christian readers alike have long seen in Amos a model of the prophet as social critic.

words.d: in the prophets, fair courts and fair dealing, especially toward people without power; Hebrew mishpat
doing what is right toward others; often paired with justice in the prophets; Hebrew tzedakah
a royal shrine of the northern kingdom of Israel where Amos spoke

look.title: Amos 5:24
look.text: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
look.prompt: The KJV says "judgment" where most modern translations say "justice." Why might a river be a good picture for either word?

check.q: According to Amos 2:6, what were the wealthy of Israel doing?
choices: Selling the needy for a pair of sandals
check.why: Amos 2:6 charges Israel with selling the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.

check.q: How does Amos use the oracles against the nations in chapters 1 and 2?
choices: He condemns the neighbors first, then turns the same judgment on Israel
He praises Israel for defeating its neighbors
He predicts Assyria will be destroyed
He lists the nations Israel should ally with
check.why: The neighbors are judged one by one, and then the longest oracle falls on Israel, catching the audience off guard.

check.q: What does Amos say about the people's feasts and songs?
choices: They should be held more often
God rejects them while justice is missing
They must move from Bethel to Jerusalem
They are acceptable if the priests are honest
check.why: Amos 5 says God will not accept the offerings or hear the songs; the demand that follows is for justice.

lessons.title: Hosea's Marriage
lessons.mainIdea: Hosea turns his own painful marriage into a picture of the bond between God and Israel.
reading: Hosea spoke in the northern kingdom in the years before it fell to Assyria in 722 BCE. His book begins with a shocking command. The text says God told Hosea to marry a woman named Gomer, who would be unfaithful, and to give their children symbolic names. One child is called Lo-ammi, "not my people." The marriage becomes a living sign. Israel, the book says, has left God for other gods the way a spouse leaves a marriage.

Readers have handled this image with care. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters have read the marriage as a real event; others read it as a parable, a story told to make a point. Modern readers also note that the image treats the nation as an unfaithful wife and God as the wronged husband, and they ask what that picture assumes about women. Studying the text means noticing both the power of the image and its cost.

The book does not end in anger. In chapter 11 the picture changes. God is a parent who taught Ephraim (another name for Israel) to walk and lifted the child to his cheek. The text has God ask, "How can I give you up?" In chapter 6 comes a line that Jewish and Christian readers both treasure: God desires steadfast love, *hesed*, rather than sacrifice. The Gospel of Matthew reports Jesus quoting it twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

words.d: Hebrew for steadfast love or loyal kindness, the loyalty a covenant partner owes
the largest northern tribe; the prophets use the name for the whole northern kingdom of Israel
a short story told to make a point, which some readers think Hosea's marriage is

look.title: Hosea 6:6
look.text: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
look.prompt: The KJV's "mercy" translates hesed. Does the line reject sacrifice, or rank it below something else? Use the words "more than" in your answer.

check.q: What does the name Lo-ammi mean?
check.why: Hosea 1 names the child Lo-ammi, "not my people," as a sign of the broken bond between God and Israel.

check.q: In Hosea 11, what picture replaces the marriage image?
choices: A parent teaching a child to walk
check.why: Hosea 11 pictures God as a parent who taught Ephraim to walk and cannot give the child up.

check.q: Which Gospel reports Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6?
check.why: Matthew 9:13 and 12:7 have Jesus cite "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."

lessons.title: Micah's Short Answer
lessons.mainIdea: Micah 6:8 sums up what the prophets ask: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly.
reading: Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in Judah, and spoke in the late 700s BCE, around the same time as Isaiah of Jerusalem. Like Amos, he attacks leaders who seize fields and houses and judges who take bribes. He is remembered for two things. He announced that Jerusalem would be plowed like a field (Micah 3:12), a line the book of Jeremiah later quotes. And he gave the shortest summary of prophetic religion in the Bible.

Chapter 6 is built as a *lawsuit*. God calls the mountains as witnesses and asks the people what he has done to wear them out. The people answer with a question: what should we bring? Burnt offerings? Thousands of rams? Rivers of oil? Even a firstborn child? The questions climb higher and higher. Then the answer comes, plain and short. God has already told you what is good: do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8).

The three verbs matter. "Do" justice is action in the courts and the market. "Love" kindness uses hesed, the loyal love Hosea spoke of. "Walk humbly" describes a way of living, not a single act. Jewish tradition cites Micah 6:8 as a summary of the commandments; the Talmud reports a rabbi who said Micah reduced the whole Torah to these three. Many Christian churches print the verse on their walls.

words.d: a prophetic form in which God brings a case against the people, with witnesses, charges and a verdict; Hebrew riv
the small Judean town Micah came from
an animal sacrifice burned whole on the altar

look.title: Micah 6:8
look.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
look.prompt: Name the three actions the verse asks for. Which of the three would be hardest to check from the outside, and why?

check.q: Micah 6 is shaped as which prophetic form?
choices: A lawsuit with witnesses and charges
check.why: Micah 6:1-2 calls the mountains as witnesses and states God's case, the pattern scholars call the covenant lawsuit.

check.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three things Micah 6:8 asks for?
check.why: The thousands of rams are among the people's offers in 6:7; the answer in 6:8 asks instead for justice, kindness and humility.

check.q: Which later book quotes Micah's warning that Jerusalem would be plowed like a field?
check.why: Jeremiah 26:18 cites Micah 3:12 when Jeremiah is on trial for saying something similar.

lessons.title: Isaiah and the Assyrians
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah of Jerusalem spoke during the Assyrian crisis and told kings to trust God rather than alliances.
reading: The book of Isaiah has 66 chapters, and most scholars think they come from more than one time. Chapters 1 through 39 are largely tied to a prophet in Jerusalem in the late 700s BCE, often called First Isaiah or Isaiah of Jerusalem. Chapter 6 tells his call: in the year King Uzziah died, he saw the LORD on a throne, heard the seraphim cry "Holy, holy, holy," and answered, "Here am I; send me."

His years were the age of *Assyria*. In 722 BCE the Assyrians destroyed Samaria and ended the northern kingdom. In 701 BCE King Sennacherib marched on Judah and besieged Jerusalem. Assyrian records and Isaiah 36 and 37 both describe the campaign, though they tell it differently: Sennacherib's inscription boasts that he shut Hezekiah up like a bird in a cage, while Isaiah says the city was spared. When two ancient sources differ, historians compare them rather than choosing one blindly.

Isaiah's message to kings was political. In chapter 7 he tells King Ahaz not to panic before a coalition of Israel and Syria. In chapters 30 and 31 he warns Hezekiah not to lean on Egypt's horses and chariots. Trust, he says, belongs to God, not to alliances. He also shares Amos's concern for the poor: chapter 1 says the people should seek justice, defend the orphan and plead for the widow, and that God is weary of their sacrifices without it.

Isaiah is also the prophet of hope. Chapter 2 pictures a day when nations beat their swords into plowshares and study war no more, a line carved on a wall across from the United Nations in New York. Chapter 11 pictures a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David's father, ruling with justice while the wolf lives with the lamb. Jews and Christians have both read these pictures as promises, and have differed on when and in whom they are fulfilled.

words.d: the empire based in northern Mesopotamia that destroyed Samaria in 722 BCE and attacked Jerusalem in 701 BCE
a scholars' name for Isaiah 1-39, tied mainly to a prophet in Jerusalem in the late 700s BCE
the fiery winged beings in Isaiah's vision who cry "Holy, holy, holy"
the Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE

look.title: Two Accounts of One Siege
look.text: Sennacherib's own inscription, carved on a clay prism now in museums, says he shut King Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage" and took tribute from him. Isaiah 37 says the Assyrian army was struck in the night and Sennacherib went home without taking the city. Both agree that Assyria surrounded Jerusalem in 701 BCE and that the city was not destroyed.
look.prompt: List what the two sources agree on and where they differ. What might each writer have wanted his readers to think?

check.q: Which chapters of Isaiah do scholars usually tie to Isaiah of Jerusalem in the 700s BCE?
check.why: First Isaiah is the usual name for chapters 1-39; chapters 40-55 are tied to the Babylonian exile.

check.q: What happened in 722 BCE?
choices: Assyria destroyed Samaria and ended the northern kingdom
Isaiah was called in the temple
check.why: Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BCE; Jerusalem fell to Babylon more than a century later.

check.q: What did Isaiah tell King Hezekiah about Egypt?
choices: Send the temple treasure to Egypt
Do not rely on Egypt's horses and chariots
check.why: Isaiah 30-31 warns against leaning on Egypt; trust belongs to God, not to alliances.

lessons.title: Comfort from Babylon
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 40-55 speaks to exiles in Babylon, announcing comfort, return, and a God who rules all nations.
reading: Isaiah 40 opens with a new tone: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people." The setting has changed. Jerusalem has already fallen; the people are in Babylon; and Cyrus, the Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, is named as God's anointed (Isaiah 45:1). For these reasons most scholars since the 1800s have read chapters 40 through 55 as the work of an unnamed prophet of the *exile*, called Second Isaiah for convenience. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have often held that the whole book comes from the eighth-century prophet, who foresaw these events. Both views are held today, and this course describes them rather than deciding between them.

The poetry of these chapters is some of the most admired in the Bible. Grass withers and flowers fade, but God's word stands. Those who wait on the LORD renew their strength and rise on wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:31). The prophet mocks idols made by carpenters and insists that there is one God who made the ends of the earth and who calls the nations to account. Many scholars see here the clearest statement of *monotheism* in the Hebrew Bible.

Second Isaiah also describes a road home. God will make a highway through the desert, lift the valleys and lower the hills, and lead the people back to Zion (Isaiah 40:3-5). In Jewish liturgy, chapters from this part of Isaiah are read as the "consolation" readings in the weeks after Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the temple. Christians hear the same chapters in Advent, and Handel set several of them in the oratorio Messiah (1741).

words.d: the removal of Judah's people to Babylon after Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BCE
a scholars' name for Isaiah 40-55, which addresses the exiles in Babylon
the belief that there is only one God
the Persian king who took Babylon in 539 BCE and allowed exiles to return; Isaiah 45 calls him God's anointed

look.title: How Scholars Divide Isaiah
look.cite: A common three-part division proposed by Bernhard Duhm in 1892 and widely used since; traditional readers treat the book as one
look.prompt: Why might a scholar look at names like Cyrus and a changed setting to date a text? What would a traditional reader say in reply?

check.q: Which Persian king is named in Isaiah 45 as God's anointed?
check.why: Isaiah 45:1 names Cyrus, who took Babylon in 539 BCE; Nebuchadnezzar was the Babylonian king who destroyed Jerusalem.

check.q: Why do many scholars date Isaiah 40-55 to the exile?
choices: Jerusalem has already fallen and Cyrus is named
The chapters are written in Greek
They describe the building of Solomon's temple
check.why: The setting is Babylon after the fall of Jerusalem, and Cyrus (539 BCE) is named, which points to the exile.

check.q: How is the exile part of Isaiah used in Jewish liturgy?
choices: Read at Passover with the Exodus story
Read as consolation in the weeks after Tisha B'Av
check.why: The seven consolation readings after Tisha B'Av come from Isaiah 40 onward.

lessons.title: The Servant Songs
lessons.mainIdea: Four poems in Second Isaiah describe a suffering servant, whom Jews and Christians have identified differently.
reading: Within Isaiah 40 through 55 are four poems about a figure called "the servant of the LORD." Scholars since Duhm (1892) have called them the *Servant Songs*: Isaiah 42:1-4, 49:1-6, 50:4-9, and 52:13 through 53:12. The servant is chosen, brings justice to the nations, is despised and beaten, suffers for others, and is finally vindicated. The fourth song is the longest. It says the servant was wounded for our transgressions and that by his stripes we are healed.

Who is the servant? The text itself gives more than one clue. In Isaiah 49:3 the servant is called Israel by name. Jewish readers, from the medieval commentators Rashi and Ibn Ezra to most Jewish readers today, have read the servant as the people of Israel, suffering in exile among the nations and later restored. On this reading the "we" who speak in chapter 53 are the nations, amazed at Israel's survival.

Christian readers, from the New Testament on, have read the fourth song as a description of Jesus. Acts 8 tells of an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot, and Philip explaining it as about Jesus. Christian worship has used the passage on Good Friday for centuries, and Handel's Messiah sets it to music. Some ancient Jewish readings also connected the servant with a messiah, and some Christian scholars accept the collective reading. The two traditions read the same words and reach different conclusions.

A public-school class does not decide who the servant is. It learns to see what each reading rests on: the name Israel in 49:3, the singular "he" of chapter 53, the speakers, the history of exile. Reading closely means holding both readings in view and being able to explain each one fairly.

words.d: four poems in Isaiah 42, 49, 50 and 52-53 about the servant of the LORD
shown to be right or innocent after suffering
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040-1105), the most read Jewish commentator on the Bible
Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one"; a hoped-for deliverer, understood differently in Jewish and Christian tradition

look.title: Isaiah 53:5
look.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
look.prompt: Read the verse twice: once with "he" as Israel among the nations, once with "he" as Jesus. What changes in who "we" are?

check.q: Which verse names the servant as Israel?
check.why: Isaiah 49:3 says "Thou art my servant, O Israel," the key text for the collective reading.

check.q: How have most Jewish readers understood the servant of Isaiah 53?
choices: As the people of Israel in exile
check.why: From Rashi and Ibn Ezra onward, the main Jewish reading takes the servant as Israel among the nations.

check.q: Which New Testament book shows Philip explaining Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official?
check.why: Acts 8 tells the story of the official reading Isaiah in his chariot.

lessons.title: Jeremiah's Call
lessons.mainIdea: Jeremiah was called young, protested, and spent forty years delivering a message his people did not want.
reading: The book of Jeremiah dates his call to the thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 627 BCE. The text says the word of the LORD came to him: before you were formed in the womb I knew you, and I appointed you a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah objected that he could not speak, for he was only a youth. The answer was that God would put words in his mouth, to pluck up and to break down, to build and to plant (Jeremiah 1:4-10).

His career ran through the last forty years of the kingdom of Judah. He watched Josiah's reforms, Josiah's death in 609 BCE, the rise of Babylon, the first deportation in 597 BCE, and the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BCE. His message was that Babylon was God's instrument and that resistance would fail. Kings and officials called that treason. He was beaten, put in stocks, and lowered into a muddy cistern to die, until an Ethiopian court official named Ebed-melech pulled him out (Jeremiah 38).

Jeremiah is the most personal of the prophets. Scattered through chapters 11 to 20 are poems scholars call his "confessions," in which he complains to God about his task. He says the word burns in his bones like fire and he cannot hold it in. He even curses the day he was born. The book also names his scribe, *Baruch*, who wrote down his words on a scroll that King Jehoiakim cut up and burned piece by piece; Jeremiah dictated it again (Jeremiah 36).

words.d: king of Judah (c. 640-609 BCE) who led a religious reform; Jeremiah was called in his reign
Jeremiah's scribe, who wrote his words on a scroll
a pit dug to store water; Jeremiah was lowered into an empty one
a scholars' name for Jeremiah's poems of complaint to God in chapters 11-20

look.title: A Young Man Objects
look.text: Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.
look.prompt: Compare this with Isaiah's "Here am I; send me" (Isaiah 6:8). What do the two call stories tell you about how each book presents its prophet?

check.q: In which king's reign does the book date Jeremiah's call?
check.why: Jeremiah 1:2 dates the call to the thirteenth year of Josiah, about 627 BCE.

check.q: What did King Jehoiakim do with Jeremiah's scroll?
choices: Read it aloud to the people
Cut it up and burned it
check.why: Jeremiah 36 says the king burned the scroll piece by piece, and Jeremiah dictated it again to Baruch.

check.q: Why did officials treat Jeremiah as a traitor?
choices: He said resisting Babylon would fail
check.why: Jeremiah told Judah that Babylon was God's instrument and that fighting it was hopeless, which leaders heard as treason.

lessons.title: The Temple Sermon
lessons.mainIdea: Jeremiah told worshippers the temple would not save them, and was nearly executed for saying it.
reading: Jeremiah 7 records a sermon at the gate of the *temple* in Jerusalem, and chapter 26 tells what happened afterward. The people, Jeremiah says, keep repeating "the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD," as if the building itself were a guarantee. He tells them these are deceptive words. If they do not deal justly, if they oppress the stranger, the orphan and the widow, the temple will not protect them.

Then he points to history. Shiloh, in the north, had once held the ark of the covenant, and Shiloh lay in ruins. God would do to this house, Jeremiah says, what he did to Shiloh. He also accuses the people of turning the temple into a den of robbers, a phrase the Gospels later have Jesus repeat in the temple courts (Mark 11:17). Chapter 26 reports that priests and prophets seized Jeremiah and demanded his death.

Jeremiah's life was saved by a precedent. Some elders reminded the crowd that Micah of Moresheth had said, a century before, that Zion would be plowed like a field, and King Hezekiah had not killed him but had listened. Jeremiah was released. The scene shows how the prophets read one another and how a community argued over what to do with an unwelcome message.

words.d: the house of worship in Jerusalem built by Solomon and destroyed by Babylon in 587 or 586 BCE
a northern shrine that once held the ark; by Jeremiah's day it was in ruins
an earlier case that guides how a later case is decided

look.title: Jeremiah 7:4
look.text: Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these.
look.prompt: Why does Jeremiah repeat the phrase three times? What is he saying the people are trusting in, and what does he say they should do instead?

check.q: What did the people mean by repeating "the temple of the LORD"?
choices: They wanted to build a second temple
check.why: Jeremiah 7 attacks the idea that the temple itself protected the city regardless of how people lived.

check.q: Why did Jeremiah mention Shiloh?
choices: It was a former shrine that now lay in ruins
It was the capital of Assyria
check.why: Shiloh had held the ark and been destroyed; Jeremiah says the temple could meet the same fate.

check.q: What saved Jeremiah from execution in chapter 26?
choices: Elders recalled that Hezekiah had spared Micah
check.why: Jeremiah 26:17-19 has elders cite Micah 3:12 as a precedent for hearing a prophet rather than killing him.

lessons.title: A New Covenant
lessons.mainIdea: Jeremiah promises a covenant written on the heart, a passage Jews and Christians have read in different ways.
reading: Jeremiah's book is mostly warning, but chapters 30 to 33 are often called the Book of Consolation. Here the prophet buys a field in his hometown while Jerusalem is under siege, as a sign that houses and fields will be bought again (Jeremiah 32). And here he speaks of a *new covenant*. A covenant is a binding agreement; the Hebrew Bible tells of God's covenant with Israel at Sinai, written on tablets of stone.

In Jeremiah 31:31-34 the text has God promise a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. It will not be like the one made at the exodus, which the people broke. This time God will put his law within them and write it on their hearts. Everyone will know God, from the least to the greatest, and sins will be forgiven. The passage stays inside Israel's story: it is a renewal of the bond with the same people and the same Torah.

Christians gave this phrase a central place. The Gospel of Luke and Paul's first letter to the Corinthians both have Jesus speak of a new covenant in his blood at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). The Letter to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 in full. The Christian name for its scriptures, the New Testament, means new covenant. Jewish readers have read the same passage as a promise of restoration after exile and of a Torah so deeply learned that it needs no teacher. Both readings start from the same verses.

words.d: a binding agreement; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel
Jeremiah 31's promise of a renewed bond written on the heart; Christians apply the phrase to Jesus, and "New Testament" translates it
a name readers give Jeremiah 30-33, the book's chapters of hope

look.title: Jeremiah 31:33
look.text: But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
look.prompt: What is the difference between a law written on stone and a law written on the heart? Which words in the verse show that the covenant is still with Israel?

check.q: What sign did Jeremiah give during the siege of Jerusalem?
choices: He bought a field in his hometown
check.why: Jeremiah 32 tells how he bought a field at Anathoth as a sign that fields would be bought again.

check.q: Where does Jeremiah 31 say the new covenant will be written?
choices: On the hearts of the people
On a scroll kept by Baruch
check.why: Jeremiah 31:33 says God will write the law on their hearts, in contrast with the tablets of Sinai.

check.q: Which book quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full?
check.why: The Letter to the Hebrews (chapter 8) quotes the whole new covenant passage.

lessons.title: Ezekiel's Visions
lessons.mainIdea: Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles, saw visions of a moving throne, dry bones, and a rebuilt temple.
reading: Ezekiel was a priest carried to Babylon in the first deportation of 597 BCE. His book dates his call to 593 BCE, by the river Chebar. He is the first prophet whose whole career took place outside the land of Israel. The book opens with a *vision* so strange that later Jewish tradition limited who could study it: a storm cloud, four living creatures with four faces each, wheels within wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with a figure like a human form in fire and light.

Ezekiel's visions are reports, not riddles. He describes what he saw, often with the phrase "the hand of the LORD was upon me." In chapters 8 through 11 he is carried in a vision to Jerusalem and watches the glory of God leave the temple. That, for Ezekiel, is why the city will fall. He also acts out his message: he lies on his side for many days, shaves his head with a sword, and packs an exile's bag in front of his neighbors.

After the fall of Jerusalem, his message turns to hope. In chapter 37 he is set down in a valley of dry bones and asked whether they can live. He prophesies, the bones rattle together, flesh covers them, and breath enters them. The text explains: the bones are the whole house of Israel, and God will bring the people back to their land. The vision has been read as national restoration, and by later Jewish and Christian readers as a picture of resurrection. The book closes with nine chapters describing a new temple, measured wall by wall.

words.d: a prophetic form in which the prophet reports what he was shown, often with an explanation
a canal near Babylon where Ezekiel lived among the exiles and saw his first vision
in Ezekiel, the visible presence of God, which he sees leave the temple and later return
the dead coming back to life; a later reading of Ezekiel's dry bones

look.title: Can These Bones Live?

check.why: Ezekiel 1 places him by the river Chebar in Babylon in 593 BCE, after the deportation of 597.

check.q: What does Ezekiel 37 say the dry bones represent?
check.why: Ezekiel 37:11 explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel, who say their hope is lost.

choices: With a detailed vision of a new temple
check.why: Ezekiel 40-48 describes a new temple and land, measured in detail.

lessons.title: How Prophets Speak
lessons.mainIdea: Prophetic books use recognizable forms: the oracle, the woe, the lawsuit and the vision report.
reading: Prophetic books can feel like a jumble of speeches. They become easier to read once you can name the forms. The basic unit is the oracle, a message delivered as God's word. It often opens with "Thus says the LORD" and closes with "says the LORD." Oracles of judgment state a charge and announce a consequence. Oracles of salvation announce rescue and often begin "Do not fear." Both kinds sit side by side in Isaiah and Jeremiah.

The *woe* is a cry of grief turned into an accusation. "Woe to those who join house to house," says Isaiah 5:8, against landowners who swallow up their neighbors' fields. Amos 6:1 says woe to those who are at ease in Zion. The word imitates the wail at a funeral, so a woe treats the guilty as already dead. The lawsuit, seen in Micah 6 and Hosea 4, uses the language of a courtroom: a summons, witnesses, charges, and a verdict.

The vision report tells what the prophet saw and how it was explained. Amos 7 through 9 has a set of them: locusts, fire, a plumb line held against a wall, a basket of summer fruit. Zechariah and Ezekiel are full of them. Add the sign-act, in which the prophet does something in public (Jeremiah's yoke, Ezekiel's packed bag), and you have most of the toolbox. Naming the form helps you ask the right question: who is charged, what is announced, and to whom.

words.d: a prophetic form that begins with a funeral cry and names the guilty, as in Isaiah 5 and Amos 6
a public action a prophet performs to deliver a message, such as Ezekiel packing an exile's bag
a weighted cord used to test whether a wall is straight; in Amos 7 a picture of judgment

look.title: Name the Form
look.text: Passage A: "Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on Mount Samaria, who oppress the poor... the days are coming when you will be taken away with hooks" (after Amos 4:1-2). Passage B: "Hear what the LORD says: Rise, plead your case before the mountains... for the LORD has a dispute with his people" (after Micah 6:1-2). Passage C: "Thus the Lord GOD showed me, and behold, a basket of summer fruit. And he said, Amos, what do you see?" (after Amos 8:1-2).
look.prompt: Match each passage to a form: oracle of judgment, lawsuit, vision report. What words gave each one away?

check.q: Which phrase usually opens an oracle?
check.why: The messenger formula "Thus says the LORD" marks a message delivered as God's word.

check.q: Where does the word "woe" come from in prophetic speech?
check.why: The woe echoes the wail of mourners, treating the guilty as if already dead.

check.q: Amos 7 shows the prophet a plumb line. What form is this?
check.why: Amos 7-9 is a series of vision reports: locusts, fire, a plumb line, summer fruit.

lessons.title: The Prophets in Birmingham
lessons.mainIdea: Civil rights leaders read Amos, Micah and Isaiah as a language for justice, and their words shaped the movement.
reading: In April 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. sat in a jail cell in Birmingham, Alabama, answering eight white clergymen who had called his campaign unwise and untimely. In the "Letter from Birmingham Jail" he accepted the label they gave him. Was he an extremist? Then so was Amos, who said let justice roll down like waters. King placed himself in a line of prophets who spoke unwelcome words to comfortable people.

Four months later, at the March on Washington, he quoted Amos 5:24 again, and the speech ended with the words of Isaiah 40: every valley exalted, every hill made low, the glory of the LORD revealed. King's audience included Black churchgoers who had sung these texts for generations and white listeners who knew them from their own churches. The prophets gave the movement a shared vocabulary. Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel, who marched beside King at Selma in 1965, had written a major study called The Prophets (1962); he said that marching there felt like praying with his legs.

Chicago felt this directly. In 1966 King moved into an apartment on the city's West Side to lead the Chicago Freedom Movement for open housing. He was struck by a rock during a march in Marquette Park. The Reverend Jesse Jackson, who had worked with King, led Operation Breadbasket in Chicago in those years. Black churches on the South and West Sides preached the prophets through it all. To study Amos in an Illinois classroom is to study a text that has been at work in the state's own history.

The prophets have been read in other movements too, from abolition to labor to the environment, and by people who disagree with one another about politics. The texts do not belong to one side. What they offer is a form: a voice that names the powerful, defends the weak, and calls for a change that flows like water.

words.d: King's 1963 open letter defending nonviolent protest, which cites Amos
a rabbi and scholar (1907-1972) who wrote The Prophets and marched with King at Selma
the 1966 campaign for open housing in Chicago that King helped lead

look.title: An Old Line in a New Speech
look.text: Amos, at Bethel, c. 760 BCE: worship without justice is rejected; let justice roll down like waters. King, in Washington, 1963: the movement will not rest until justice rolls down like waters. Same words, new city, new listeners. The first audience was a prosperous kingdom soon to fall to Assyria; the second was a nation debating a civil rights bill that Congress passed in 1964.
look.prompt: What does King keep from Amos, and what does he change by placing the line in his own speech? Who is "the powerful" in each setting?

check.q: In the "Letter from Birmingham Jail," how does King respond to being called an extremist?
choices: He says Amos was also an extremist for justice
He denies the charge and promises to be moderate
He says the label came from Babylon
check.why: King accepts the label and lists Amos among others who were extremists for justice.

check.q: Which rabbi and author of The Prophets marched with King at Selma?
check.why: Heschel published The Prophets in 1962 and marched at Selma in 1965.

check.q: What was the goal of the 1966 Chicago Freedom Movement?
check.why: King moved to Chicago's West Side in 1966 to campaign for open housing.

review.q: Which prophet was a herdsman from Tekoa who spoke at Bethel?
review.why: Amos 1:1 and 7:14 describe him as a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who spoke in the northern kingdom.

review.q: Hosea's marriage to Gomer is used in the book as what?
choices: A living sign of the bond between God and Israel
review.why: Hosea 1-3 makes the marriage a sign of Israel's unfaithfulness and God's steadfast love.

review.q: Micah 6:8 asks the reader to do justice, love kindness and what?
review.why: The three demands are to do justice, love hesed, and walk humbly; the offerings are what the people propose and the verse sets aside.

review.q: How do Jewish and Christian readers differ on the servant of Isaiah 53?
choices: Jews read it as Cyrus; Christians as Isaiah himself
Jewish readers mostly see Israel; Christians see Jesus
Jews read it as Jesus; Christians as Israel
review.why: The main Jewish reading takes the servant as Israel among the nations; the Christian reading since the New Testament sees Jesus.

review.q: What is the name of the Persian king who took Babylon in 539 BCE and is called God's anointed in Isaiah 45?
review.why: Isaiah 45:1 names Cyrus; Sennacherib was Assyrian and Nebuchadnezzar Babylonian.

review.q: Jeremiah's temple sermon warned that the temple would become like which place?
review.why: Jeremiah 7:12-14 points to Shiloh, a former shrine that lay in ruins.

review.q: The dry bones of Ezekiel 37 are explained in the text as which of these?
review.why: Ezekiel 37:11 says the bones are the whole house of Israel, who will be brought back to their land.

review.q: A passage that begins with a funeral cry and names the guilty is which form?
review.why: The woe, as in Isaiah 5 and Amos 6, borrows the cry of mourning to accuse the living.
